newsitem.title: UK: Sterling plays catch up on the mark.
newsitem.headline: Sterling plays catch up on the mark.

text.p: Sterling has romped up five percent against the mark over the past couple of months having played catch-up on a relative value basis with the likes of the lira, and simply because it has been undervalued, analysts said on Wednesday.

European economic and monetary union (EMU) convergence trades picked up in early September in the run up to the French budget when many in the market became convinced that budgets could be juggled sufficiently for a broad based EMU to go ahead in 1999.
This prompted a convergence boom in currencies and bonds of countries it was hitherto thought would not make EMU, most notably Italy, Spain, Sweden and Finland.

Even though few believe Britain will be in the first EMU group, sound fundamentals mean it did not make sense for sterling and British governemnt bonds (gilts) be left behind. "What we are seeing is the U.K. catching up with some of this convergence euphoria," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

The government's wait-and-see stance to EMU -- not to mention the fact that the chance of sterling going back into the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) in the near-term to fulfil that part of the Maastricht critera is practially zero -- means Britain is not expected to be part of the first EMU group.

But eventually when you have one market standing still and others rushing off down the track, relative yields and currency levels start to make no sense and the lagging market, in this case the U.K., gets carried along.

"Within Europe the U.K. is too big a market to get left behind, it would be fair if it had lousy fundamentals but it doesn't," Coleman added. The very fact that there are doubts Britain will not be part of EMU in the near-term is a nice hedge for investors wanting to cash in on the convergence trades but not wanting to be exposed to currencies and bonds that might take a big hit if the process runs into serious trouble.

Italian and Spanish bonds markets (Btp and Bonos) are very firm on the Herculean efforts being made on budgets to meet the Maastricht critera but both are seen as being seriously at risk should EMU crumble.
"Gilts have stood still for a long time while others like Btps and Bonos have rallied massively," said Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust.
"On a relative basis gilts look pretty good value and sterling still looks reasonably cheap at these levels. There's still a chance that EMU is delayed and you could get a big correction elsewhere."
All this is happening against the backdrop of good economic fundamentals with growth picking up and inflation staying reasonably low and no blow-out in the balance of payments, yet.

"The underlying outlook for the economy has been better than it has been for sometime," said Kevin Gardiner, international economist at Morgan Stanley, who expressed little concern over sterling's old Achilles' heel, the balance of payments.
The looming general election is also not causing investors huge jitters, even if it results in a change of government.

Labour's shadow chancellor Gordon Brown seems in large part to go along with the existing marco-economic policy stance of Chancellor Kenneth Clarke so the economic status-quo will likely be maintained.

"I feel that Labour are going to be less market friendly than the Conservatives but there is less in it than there has ever been. You have never seen the two main political parties in the U.K. this close together.
"You can talk about political convergence even if you can't talk about monetary and economic convergence."
